items.title: What Pasteur first pasteurised
items.claim: Louis Pasteur developed pasteurisation in the 1860s. What was he originally trying to preserve?
items.reveal_title: Pasteurisation began with wine, not milk
items.reveal:
Pasteur's 1866 work Etudes sur le vin addressed spoilage in French wines. He showed heating to about 50-60 C killed the microbes that caused spoilage without ruining flavour.

Milk pasteurisation became widespread later, accelerated by urban infant mortality concerns from the 1890s.
items.why: Technologies often arrive in industries far from where they were originally invented.

items.title: The MSG 'syndrome' myth
items.claim: The idea that monosodium glutamate causes a distinctive 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' came from a 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine. What does the controlled evidence show?

options.text: Robust evidence MSG causes the symptoms in most people
Double-blind trials have not consistently linked MSG within typical food levels to the reported symptoms
MSG is toxic at any dose

items.reveal_title: The popular reaction outran the evidence
items.reveal:
Reviews including the US Food and Drug Administration's classification of MSG as 'Generally Recognised As Safe' (GRAS) and double-blind challenge studies have not consistently reproduced the symptoms at dietary doses.

Kikunae Ikeda first isolated glutamate as the source of umami in 1908 at Tokyo Imperial University.
items.why: A high-profile anecdote can shape food policy and public perception for decades.

items.title: The cold chain's wider effect
items.claim: Mechanical refrigeration became common in 20th-century homes and supply chains. Beyond food preservation, what is one less-obvious effect?

options.text: It made beef cheaper to ship from Argentina to Europe, restructuring agriculture in both regions
It eliminated the need for canning

items.reveal:
Refrigerated ships from the 1880s onwards allowed Argentine, Australian and New Zealand meat exports to Britain, reshaping rural economies and diets.

Domestic refrigerators became common in US homes in the 1930s-1950s and in the UK from the 1960s.
items.why: Food technologies reorganise economies, not just kitchens.

items.title: Why we cure meat with nitrites
items.claim: Sodium nitrite is used in cured meats partly for colour and flavour. What is its main food-safety function?
items.reveal:
C. botulinum produces one of the most lethal toxins known. Nitrites suppress its growth in the anaerobic conditions inside cured meats.

The IARC classified processed meat as Group 1 carcinogenic to humans in 2015 partly due to nitrite and nitrate residues; risks and benefits are now actively traded off in regulation.
items.why: Food additives often combine functional safety roles with health trade-offs.

items.title: The first cultured meat burger
items.claim: The first publicly cooked and tasted cultured meat burger was presented in London in 2013. Roughly what did it cost to produce?
items.reveal_title: About a third of a million dollars per burger
items.reveal:
Mark Post's 5 August 2013 demonstration used cultured bovine muscle cells. The project was funded by Sergey Brin.

By 2023 Singapore and the US approved limited cultured chicken sales; production costs remain orders of magnitude above conventional meat.
items.why: Technologies start at extreme costs that fall steeply if scale is achieved.

items.title: Where Quorn comes from
items.claim: Quorn is a protein source first sold in 1985. What is it?

options.text: Mycoprotein from the fungus Fusarium venenatum

items.reveal_title: A fungus discovered in a Buckinghamshire soil sample
items.reveal:
Rank Hovis McDougall identified the strain in the 1960s. After two decades of safety testing, mycoprotein launched commercially as Quorn in 1985.

The organism is grown in fermenters on glucose feedstock.
items.why: Some staple ingredients require decades of work before reaching shelves.

items.title: Organic vs conventional yields
items.claim: Meta-analyses have compared organic and conventional crop yields globally. What do they typically find?

options.text: Organic yields are on average around 20-25% lower with substantial variation by crop and system

items.reveal:
Seufert et al. (2012, Nature) and Ponisio et al. (2015) found organic yields averaged 19-25% lower, with smaller gaps for legumes and in some agroforestry systems.

Land-use, biodiversity and pollution trade-offs complicate any single yardstick.
items.why: Agricultural decisions involve trade-offs across multiple metrics, not a single optimisation.

items.title: Industrial trans fats banned
items.claim: Industrial trans fats from partial hydrogenation were once common in margarine and processed food. Denmark was first to set strict national limits. In which year?
items.reveal_title: Denmark restricted industrial trans fats in 2003
items.reveal:
The US FDA effectively eliminated artificial trans fats by 2018. WHO's REPLACE programme set global elimination targets.

Mortality modelling estimated tens of thousands of cardiovascular deaths prevented in Denmark alone.
items.why: Public-health regulation can change food formulations across an entire economy.

items.title: Coeliac disease prevalence
items.claim: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten. What is the approximate population prevalence in Western countries based on serological screening?
items.reveal:
Singh et al. (2018, meta-analysis) reported a global pooled seroprevalence of 1.4% and biopsy-confirmed prevalence of 0.7%. Most cases remain undiagnosed.

Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity is a separate, less well-characterised category.
items.why: Population screening reveals that some conditions are far more common than clinic-based estimates suggest.

items.title: Food miles vs diet choice
items.claim: Poore and Nemecek's 2018 Science analysis of food systems found transport accounts for what share of typical food carbon footprints?

options.text: Around 1-10% for most foods, with production stages dominating

items.reveal_title: Transport is usually a small slice; production dominates
items.reveal:
Poore and Nemecek (2018) aggregated data from over 38,000 farms. For most foods, on-farm emissions, land-use change and processing dominate. Air-freighted produce and beef from deforested land are exceptions.

Choosing what to eat typically dwarfs food miles for footprint.
items.why: Salient measures (miles travelled) can mislead about underlying impacts.

items.title: Salt iodisation
items.claim: Iodised salt was introduced as a public health measure to address iodine deficiency. In which decade did it first reach mass deployment in the US?
items.reveal:
Iodised salt was introduced commercially in Michigan in 1924, addressing goitre in the 'goitre belt'.

WHO estimates universal salt iodisation has substantially reduced the global prevalence of iodine deficiency disorders since the 1990s.
items.why: Adding a micronutrient to a staple is among the most cost-effective public-health measures recorded.

items.title: PLA composting
items.claim: Polylactic acid (PLA) is often marketed as a compostable bioplastic for food packaging. What is true of its end-of-life conditions?

options.text: It composts in any home compost bin in days
It typically requires industrial composting with controlled temperature and microbes
It does not degrade at all

items.reveal_title: Industrial composting, not the home bin
items.reveal:
PLA is certified under standards such as EN 13432 for industrial composting at around 55-60 C. In landfills and oceans it degrades slowly.

Misclassification of PLA as 'biodegradable' has been a recurring concern in waste streams.
items.why: Sustainability labels require infrastructure to deliver their promised outcomes.
